newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Europe to integrate and include Turkey.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Europe to integrate and include Turkey.

text.p: Deputy U.S. Secretary of State Strobe Talbott on Tuesday urged a deepening of ties between European countries and warned against excluding Turkey, in particular, from post-Cold War integration.

Speaking at a U.S.-European Union conference on fostering trans-Atlantic relations, Talbott backed EU monetary union and strongly endorsed European integration but laid out clear U.S. preferences for how that should be done.

Tackling the issue of Turkey specifically, he noted that some in Europe "resist vehemently the idea that any nations to the east of what might be called 'traditional Europe' can ever be part of a larger, 21st century Europe."
"We believe that view is quite wrong and potentially quite dangerous," he said, citing Turkey, which is a NATO member and has been pressing unsuccesfully to join the EU.

Many European leaders, including in Germany where the presence of thousands of Turkish workers has caused strains at a time of economic tightening, oppose Ankara's EU membership. They also cite widespread reports of human rights violations.

Talbott said: "We encourage our friends and allies in Europe to embrace the broadest, most expansive, most outward-looking, most inclusive possible version of integration." That should include expanding international institutions like the 15-member EU.
"We must continue to make sure that cooperation within regions reinforces cooperation among regions," he said.

Talbott acknowledged that Turkey, the only predominently moslem NATO member and a lynchpin of the alliance's South- eastern flank, is undergoing "the strains of modernisation, including in the crucial area of democracy and human rights."

But he insisted: "These difficulties do not make Turkey any less European. In fact, many current EU members have overcome far greater traumas in this century -- and that's putting it mildly." He said Turkey had been part of the European system since the 16th century.
Talbott also stressed the need to avoid a religious divide among "Catholic, Orthodox and Islamic parts of Europe."
On another subject of controversy associated with European integration, Talbott said the planned European economic and monetary union in 1999 could be good for the American economy.

"We have no doubt that an EMU that cements an open single market and that sparks economic growth in Europe will be good for the American economy," he told his audience of European and American officials, experts and representatives of non-governmental organisations.
"If the EU emerges from this bold initiative able to play an even more active and constructive role on the world stage, that will be good for America too," he said, adding:
"A politically united Europe will be a stronger partner to advance common goals. An economically united Europe creates a much more attractive environment for American investment."

Talbott disclosed that Washington's "ulterior motive" for pressing so hard to expand NATO to include former communist states in central and eastern Europe was to encourage enlargement of the EU as well.

He stressed the importance of bringing these emerging new democracies into the EU, as well as NATO, but said he was not criticising the pace of EU decision-making because potential new EU members must make complex changes in their systems.

The two-day conference, which aims to draw up a specific work plan of steps to strengthen and expand U.S.-Europe ties, opened on Monday with an address by Sir Leon Brittan, European trade commissioner.

He said while historical U.S.-European links were strong and deep, "they are not alone sufficient for our future." Hence, the need for the conference, which came just before the 50th anniversary on June 5 of the creation of the Marshall Plan that helped rebuild Europe after World War II.

Brittan noted that in 20 years, one in three Americans will be of non-European descent. "In the future, it is common values and aspirations, rather than common ancestry, that will unite us across the Atlantic," he said.
